claims.text: Earlier studies produced HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure containing multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The previously produced hierarchical microstructure of HfNbTiVAl10 is stable.

An integrated framework combining in situ SEM tensile testing, high-resolution DIC, nanoindentation mapping, dynamic imaging of crack-initiation zones, and a physics-informed CNN can predict macroscopic Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.

DIC, nanoindentation, and dynamic imaging can capture local strain variations, microstructural variations, grain-boundary distributions, chemical fluctuations, and transient crack-initiation features relevant to bulk behavior.
High-fidelity local experimental measurements can replace or bypass computationally intensive simulations in predicting the mechanical properties of hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
A physics-informed CNN can use local structural and deformation measurements to infer bulk mechanical properties.
Dynamic imaging of crack-initiation zones improves the capture of nonlinear fracture processes.
Improved capture of nonlinear fracture processes enhances the robustness of fracture-toughness predictions.
The framework will reduce computational demand by approximately one order of magnitude relative to prior CALPHAD, first-principles, and conventional machine-learning methods.
The framework will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–20% relative to prior methods.
Predicted Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness will each be within ±10% of prospective measured values.
Prior CALPHAD, first-principles, and conventional machine-learning approaches had lower efficiency than the proposed framework.
Prior methods were less successful at accurately predicting fracture toughness.
The framework remains reliable under controlled ambient temperature and conventional tensile and fracture-test strain rates.
The framework's reliability depends on the hierarchical heterostructure remaining stable without phase changes or significant microstructural evolution.
Severe environmental degradation such as oxidation may cause the method to fail.
Failure of the imaging system to capture dynamic crack-propagation behavior may cause the method to fail.
The estimated accuracy and efficiency gains depend on effective integration of dynamic-imaging data.
